610.title: I am the bread of life (John 6:22–51)
610.word: I am the bread of life
610.hook: the first I AM: whoever comes to me will never hunger
610.howItsDone: Christians often connect this saying with communion; in many churches, the bread is shared at the Lord's Supper, the Eucharist or Holy Communion, and many Christians also say grace before ordinary meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boat in the dark, and a voice on the water: it is I. Your line was be not afraid. When the fear showed up, did the line help? Day six hundred ten.

Next morning, the crowd from the hillside wakes up and Jesus is gone. So are the disciples. They grab whatever boats they can find and cross the lake to Capernaum looking for him. When they find him, he doesn't say welcome. He says, gently but plainly: you're not here because of the signs. You're here because you ate the bread and were filled. It's an honest thing to say to a crowd. People come back to the place they last got fed. Who doesn't? And then he tells them what he's really offering.

"Labour not for the meat which perisheth," he says, meaning food that goes stale. Work for food that lasts. The crowd brings up their history: "Our fathers did eat manna in the desert; as it is written, He gave them bread from heaven to eat." Manna, the bread that fell every morning in the wilderness, enough for one day, never more. They're asking, can you top that? Jesus says the true bread from heaven isn't something Moses gave, it's something the Father gives now. And the crowd, like the woman at the well asking for that water, says: "Lord, evermore give us this bread." Then he says it: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." This is the first of seven great sayings in John's Gospel where Jesus says I am, and then names a picture. Bread, light, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection, the way, the vine. We'll meet every one of them on this path. Bread comes first. It's the plainest thing on any table in that world, the food of every day, every family, rich and poor. Jesus doesn't say I am a feast, or I am a rare delicacy. He says I am bread. Something you need daily, that keeps you alive. Christians understand this saying in different ways. Many hear it about faith: coming to Jesus feeds a hunger nothing else fills. Catholic and Orthodox Christians, along with many others, also hear it pointing to the bread of communion. Many hear both at once. And the word that makes the saying sharp is the one he keeps returning to: life.
screen: `THE FIRST OF SEVEN I AM SAYINGS.`
then, large: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat bread slowly. If you have a piece of bread nearby, or a cracker, take it now. If not, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Look at it. Think of the wheat, the field, the person who baked it. Take one small bite and chew slowly, longer than feels normal. Notice the taste change as you chew. Notice the simple fact of being fed. Then ask what you're hungry for that bread can't fill. If you pray, you can bring that hunger to God. If you don't, simply give thanks for the bread. The bell holds the time.
I am the bread of life. The first of Jesus's seven I am sayings in John: whoever comes to him will never hunger.
screen: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bread of life. Today, at one meal, pause before the first bite and remember that you're being kept alive. Day six hundred ten.

611.title: To whom shall we go? (John 6:52–71)
611.hook: many leave; Peter says: you have the words of eternal life
611.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to Peter's words in seasons of doubt, and in some liturgies his line is sung as a verse before the Gospel is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crowd asked for manna, and Jesus said: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life. Did you pause before a meal? Day six hundred eleven.

There's a moment in a lot of friendships, and a lot of faiths, when the thing gets hard. The easy early days are over. Something is said that you can't quite follow, or can't quite accept. And you look around, and other people are quietly leaving. This is that moment in John's Gospel. Jesus has been teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum about bread from heaven, and the teaching gets stranger and stronger. Even his own followers start muttering among themselves. In the King James Bible they say: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?"

What was so hard? Jesus had said that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. His hearers take it as literally as anyone would, and they recoil. Christians have understood these words in different ways ever since. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hear in them the Eucharist, the bread and wine that become, in their teaching, the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Other Protestant churches read the words as a picture of faith: taking Christ in, the way bread is taken into the body. And in the story, the result is the same. "From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him." Not enemies. Disciples. People who had followed him. So Jesus turns to the twelve and asks: "Will ye also go away?" He doesn't beg them to stay. He doesn't soften what he said. He just asks. And Peter answers for them: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." Listen to how honest that is. Peter doesn't say, I understand everything you just said. He doesn't say, it was easy to hear. He says, where else would we go? Peter's answer isn't certainty. It's a choice about where life is, made on a day he doesn't understand everything. But John adds a sad note: Jesus already knows one of the twelve will betray him.
screen: then, large: `LORD, TO WHOM SHALL WE GO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with what gives you life. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that gives you life but has gotten hard lately. A friendship. A marriage. A practice like this one. A faith, if you have one. Notice whether part of you is tempted to walk away quietly. Don't scold it. Then ask Peter's question honestly: if I leave, where would I go? What would I lose? If you pray, you can tell God plainly what's hard. If you don't, simply hold the thing that gives you life, and choose it for today. The bell holds the time.
To whom shall we go? Peter's answer when many disciples left: thou hast the words of eternal life.
screen: `TO WHOM SHALL WE GO? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: to whom else? Today, stay one minute longer with something hard that you know gives you life. Day six hundred eleven.

612.title: Judge rightly (John 7:1–24)
612.hook: at the harvest festival of booths, he teaches in secret then openly
612.howItsDone: Christians read this chapter as part of John's story of Jesus at the great Jewish feasts; Jews today keep Sukkot each autumn by building and eating in a sukkah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many walked away, and Peter said: Lord, to whom shall we go? Your line was to whom else? What did you stay with? Day six hundred twelve.

Each autumn, Jewish families who keep Sukkot build a little hut. Walls of wood or cloth, a roof of branches loose enough to see the stars through. For a week, they eat in it, and some sleep in it. It's called a sukkah, a booth, and the festival is Sukkot, the Feast of Tabernacles. Jews still keep it today. Today's chapter of John opens as that feast approaches, and Jesus's own brothers are pushing him: go up to Jerusalem, show yourself to the world.
screen: `A HUT WITH A ROOF OF BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: John says it plainly: "Now the Jews' feast of tabernacles was at hand." Tabernacle is an old word for a tent. The law of Moses told Israel to live in booths for seven days, remembering the years in the wilderness, when God's people lived in tents and God kept them. It was also a harvest festival, the end of the year's gathering, full of joy. Jesus's brothers want him to go and make a splash, and John adds a line that's honest about family: "For neither did his brethren believe in him." Jesus tells them his time hasn't come, and stays behind. Then, after they leave, he goes up anyway, quietly, not openly. Meanwhile in Jerusalem, people are whispering about him. He's a good man. No, he's leading people astray. Halfway through the feast, he walks into the temple courts and starts teaching out loud. People are amazed: "How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?" He hasn't studied under any teacher they know. He's from Galilee. They're judging by appearances, and he knows it. Then he takes up the old argument about the healing on the sabbath. You circumcise a baby boy on the sabbath, he says, when the eighth day falls on it, so the law of Moses isn't broken. Then why are you angry with me for making a whole man well on the sabbath? It's a careful argument from inside Jewish practice. And he ends with the line this day is named for: "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment." Look past the surface. A man from Galilee with no teacher might be a teacher. A healing on the sabbath might be keeping the sabbath, not breaking it.
screen: then, large: `JUDGE NOT ACCORDING TO THE APPEARANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look beneath appearances. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've judged quickly. Maybe by their clothes, their accent, their job, or a single thing they said. Picture them clearly. Now try to imagine what you don't know. What they carry. What they've survived. What they might be good at. Let your picture of them get a little bigger. If you pray, you can ask to see them as God sees them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with more curiosity than you did a minute ago. The bell holds the time.
Feast of Tabernacles. Sukkot, the autumn harvest festival when Jewish families live in booths, remembering the wilderness. Jesus teaches openly in the temple during it.
Your line: judge not by appearance. Today, when you catch yourself sizing someone up, ask one question you don't know the answer to. Day six hundred twelve.

613.title: Rivers of living water (John 7:25–52)
613.hook: on the great day of the feast he cries: let anyone thirsty come
613.howItsDone: Christians often read this passage at Pentecost, connecting the rivers of living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit; many also connect it with baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Feast of Tabernacles, huts with roofs of branches, and a teacher with no famous teacher. Your line was judge not by appearance. What question did you ask? Day six hundred thirteen.

A golden pitcher, a pool, and a procession at dawn. According to Jewish tradition written down in the Mishnah, on the mornings of the Feast of Tabernacles a priest walked down to the pool of Siloam with a golden pitcher, filled it with water, and carried it back up to the temple, with crowds and music. At the altar, he poured the water out. In a dry land waiting for the winter rains, that poured-out water meant something. Now it's the last day of the feast, the greatest day. And in the middle of the crowds, Jesus stands up and shouts.

John writes: "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink." John notes both things: he stood, and he cried out. Then: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Belly is the old, literal word. Here it means the deepest inside of a person, which is why some modern translations say heart. And there's a puzzle here. Whose heart? The sentence can be read two ways. Rivers flowing out of the believer, or rivers flowing out of Jesus himself, for anyone who comes and drinks. Readers have taken it both ways. John explains it himself in the next verse: Jesus was speaking about the Spirit, which those who believed would receive. Notice where we've been. A woman at a well heard about living water. A crowd heard about bread. Now, at a festival of water, Jesus offers rivers. And the crowd splits. Some say he's the prophet. Some say he's the Christ. Others say, the Christ can't come from Galilee. Officers are sent to arrest him, and they come back empty-handed. Why didn't you bring him? Their answer: "Never man spake like this man." And one quiet voice speaks up on the council: Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter three. He asks a fair question: shouldn't we hear a man before judging him? He's beginning to come out of the dark.

Here's the practice: drink water with gratitude. If you have a glass of water near you, hold it. If not, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Think about where this water came from. Rain, a river, pipes under your street, the people who keep them working. Take a slow sip. Feel it go down. Notice that your body needed it, even if you didn't feel thirsty. Then think of one person near you who could use a drink, or a kind word. If you pray, you can give thanks for the water. If you don't, simply give thanks for the glass in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Rivers of living water. Jesus's cry on the last day of the feast: whoever is thirsty, come and drink, and rivers will flow from within.
Your line: out of the heart, rivers. Today, every time you drink something, give thanks once, and let one kind word flow out to someone else. Day six hundred thirteen.

614.title: Let the one without sin (John 8:1–11)
614.hook: a woman dragged before him; he writes in the dust; stones fall; a passage later manuscripts added
614.howItsDone: Christians often read this story when teaching about mercy and judging others; some churches read it during Lent, and "cast the first stone" has passed into everyday English.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last great day of the feast, and Jesus crying out: if any man thirst. Your line was out of the heart, rivers. What flowed out of you? Day six hundred fourteen.

Early morning in the temple courts. Jesus is sitting, teaching a crowd. Suddenly a group of men push through, dragging a woman, and stand her in the middle of everyone. She's been caught in adultery, they say, in the very act. Moses commanded that such should be stoned, they tell him. What do you say? The story makes clear it's a test, a trap. If he says let her go, he seems to set aside the law. If he says stone her, the teacher of mercy approves an execution. Everyone is watching. The woman is standing there, alone. And Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger.

"But Jesus stooped down, and with his finger wrote on the ground, as though he heard them not." What did he write? Nobody knows. The Gospel never says. Readers have guessed for centuries: the sins of the accusers, a verse from the prophets, nothing at all. The text keeps its secret. They keep pressing him. So he stands up and says one sentence: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." Then he bends down and writes again. And one by one, they leave, the King James says, "beginning at the eldest, even unto the last." The oldest first. Maybe because they had the longest memories of their own failures. Notice too what the story leaves out. The law named both the man and the woman. Where is he? Only she was dragged into the middle. When they've all gone, Jesus stands and speaks to her directly, maybe the first person that morning to do so. "Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?" She answers: "No man, Lord." And he says: "Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." Both halves matter. No condemnation, and a new way to live. Now the scholar's detail. Open a modern Bible and you may find this story in brackets, with a note: the oldest Greek copies of John don't have it, and later copies place it in different spots, some even in Luke. Some readers think it's an old story about Jesus that circulated on its own before it found a home in the Gospel. Churches handle the note differently. The Catholic Church holds the passage as part of scripture, and Protestant and Orthodox churches read and preach it too.
screen: then, large: `LET HIM FIRST CAST A STONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put down one stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you're holding a stone against. Someone who hurt you, failed you, or whom you've quietly decided is beyond forgiving. You don't have to forgive them completely today. Just picture the stone in your hand. Feel its weight. Then remember one of your own failures, something you'd hate dragged into the middle of a crowd. Now, if you can, open your hand and set the stone down, even for a few minutes. If you pray, you can ask for help to leave it there. If you don't, simply notice how your hand feels empty. The bell holds the time.
Let the one without sin. Jesus's answer to a crowd ready to stone a woman: let the one without sin cast the first stone.
screen: `LET THE ONE WITHOUT SIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: neither do I condemn you. Today, when you're about to condemn someone, in words or in your head, remember the stone you set down. Day six hundred fourteen.

615.title: The light of the world (John 8:12–30)
615.hook: whoever follows me won't walk in darkness
615.tomorrow: the truth will set you free
615.howItsDone: Many Christians light candles in worship as a sign of Christ as the light of the world; at the Easter Vigil in many churches, a single candle is carried into a dark church and its flame is shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman dragged into the middle, words written in the dust, and stones dropped one by one. Your line was neither do I condemn you. Did you set a stone down? Day six hundred fifteen.

Jerusalem had no streetlights. After sunset there were oil lamps, the moon, and not much else. Then, one week a year, the temple lights up. According to the Mishnah, during the Feast of Tabernacles, huge golden lampstands stood in the temple's Court of the Women, each with bowls of oil, and young priests climbed ladders to fill them. Wicks were made from the priests' worn-out garments. The tradition says there wasn't a courtyard in Jerusalem that wasn't lit by that light. People danced with torches beneath it all night. And in that same court, Jesus speaks.

"I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." This is the second of the I am sayings in John. Bread first, now light. And John tells us exactly where he said it: "These words spake Jesus in the treasury, as he taught in the temple." The treasury, where the offering chests stood, was in the Court of the Women, the same court where those great lamps burned at the feast. So picture him there, near the lampstands, saying: I am the light. Light has run through John's Gospel since its first lines. John's first lines said the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness could not grasp it or put it out. Now the light speaks for itself. Notice the shape of the promise. He doesn't say, whoever follows me will never face darkness. Night still comes. He says, they won't walk in darkness. They'll carry the light of life with them, like someone walking home at night with a lamp. The path isn't lit all the way to the end; just enough for the next step. The people listening push back. You're testifying about yourself; that doesn't count. Jesus answers that his Father bears witness with him. Who are you? they ask. And he speaks of a day when they'll lift up the Son of Man, a hint of the cross, and then they'll know. John ends this scene simply: as he spoke these words, many believed in him.
screen: then, large: `I AM THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere lit, slowly. If you can, stand and walk slowly toward a window or a lamp. If you can't move right now, turn toward the brightest thing in the room. Settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest on the light. Notice how it falls on things, how it shows you the floor, the edges, the way forward. Take a few slow steps, or simply breathe slowly, and notice you only need enough light for the next step. If you pray, you can ask for light on one part of your path. If you don't, rest in the brightness. The bell holds the time.
The light of the world. The second of Jesus's I am sayings in John, spoken in the temple where the great festival lamps burned.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the light of life. Today, when you switch on a light, pause for a second and ask what the next step is. Just the next one. Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: The truth will set you free (John 8:31–59)
616.word: The truth will set you free
616.carry: the truth shall make you free
616.howItsDone: Christians read this passage as teaching that freedom comes from staying with Jesus's word; churches today also teach clearly against using John 8 to blame or demean Jewish people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, golden lamps in the temple, and Jesus saying: I am the light of the world. Your line was the light of life. What was your next step? Day six hundred sixteen.

Some sentences escape their books. Today's has. It's carved in stone in the lobby of the CIA's original headquarters building in Virginia. It's on university buildings and library walls. In Latin, it's the motto of Johns Hopkins University. Politicians quote it, journalists quote it, people who've never opened a Bible quote it. "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." Out of context, it sounds like a slogan for information: get the facts, and you'll be free. But in John's Gospel it's the middle of a hard conversation, and the sentence before it changes everything.

Here's the sentence before: "If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed." Continue means stay, abide, live there. So the truth Jesus means isn't a fact you look up. It's something you come to know by staying close to him, the way you only really know a friend by spending years together. And the freedom he means isn't political. His hearers object: "We be Abraham's seed, and were never in bondage to any man." Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin. The freedom he offers is from the inside out. The argument gets sharp. Both sides claim Abraham. This chapter contains hard words, spoken in a fierce argument among Jews, and over the centuries some Christians twisted those words into hatred of Jewish people, with terrible results. Churches today, Catholic and Protestant, have taught clearly against that reading. Then comes the line that ends the argument: "Before Abraham was, I am." Not before Abraham was, I was. I am. The same two Greek words as the voice on the water, ego eimi. The tenses don't match, and his listeners hear it as a claim to God's own name. They pick up stones, and he slips away. Look back over this week: bread of life, Peter's to whom shall we go, judging rightly at the feast of booths, rivers of living water, a stone set down, the light of the world, and now truth that frees.
screen: then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell one freeing truth. Settle, and breathe. Think of something true that you've been avoiding saying. An apology you owe. A thank you you've never spoken. A boundary you need. Or just something true about how you feel. Notice how it sits in you, unsaid. Heavy, maybe, or tight. Imagine saying it, simply and kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Notice what loosens. If you pray, you can ask for courage and gentleness. If you don't, simply choose the words you'd use. The bell holds the time.
The truth will set you free. Jesus's promise to those who continue in his word: knowing the truth by staying close, and being freed by it.
screen: `THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the truth shall make you free. Today, say the true thing you chose, kindly, to the person who needs to hear it. Day six hundred sixteen, and another week on the path.

fork.setup: you've just said, "we were never in bondage to anyone." the argument has turned to Abraham. what does Jesus say last?
fork.reveal: "before Abraham was, I am." his listeners hear a claim to God's own name and pick up stones; he slips away.

original.note: Greek: truth. In John, truth is something you can know by staying close, not only a fact.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slogan about facts and information.
what it means: truth known by continuing in Jesus's word, and a freedom from the inside out.
what a scholar hears: "before Abraham was, I am" sets a past tense against a present one with ego eimi, and this chapter's hard words were later misused against Jews.
